rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
papers.authors: Juhana Kangaspunta, Khalil Hajji, Darshan Fofadiya, Kyumin Park, Michael Garner, Anthony Maltsev, Ryan Synk, Jose Sepulv...
papers.summary: Search and recommendation at Shopify have to retrieve relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of items under tight latency limits. This report casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens that represent products. The model is jointly pretrained on catalog and behavioral data so search and recommendation share a representation and a training objective. Reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance, and distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation without a statistically detected loss in search quality. In an online test on the home recommendation feed, adding the model raised attributed orders by 7.95%, converting users by 8.60%, and conversion rate by 9.85% on that feed.

papers.title: RedMall: Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale E-commerce
papers.authors: Kunyang Zhou, Xin Jia, Yi Yang, Yongjun Yang, Manjie Xu, Honglei Zhang, Yan Zhu, Kai Zuo, Xu Tang, Zheng Wang
papers.summary: Generative retrieval outputs a Semantic ID (SID), but several products can share one SID, and which of them are finally retrieved directly affects online gains. RedMall is a generative model for e-commerce recommendation and ad retrieval. Besides changes to the architecture and training objectives, such as treating items that were shown but not clicked as negatives, it handles this step explicitly. In serving, each product under the same SID gets a score, a weighted mix of the GMV it brought per thousand impressions in the past, weighted most, and its orders per thousand impressions, and only the top-scoring ones are kept. In the e-commerce recommendation A/B test, the full model raised GMV by 1.08%. The authors also tested this step on its own in ad retrieval: without it, the online lift in ad retrieval is no longer significant, because duplicates are filtered downstream and only about half as many items get through. ==How a SID is turned into products also decides how much generative retrieval gains==.

papers.title: Rethinking Latent Reasoning for Generative Recommendation: Beyond Teacher-Generated CoT and Recurrent Hidden-State Feedback
papers.authors: Yiwen Chen, Fuwei Zhang, Zehao Chen, Deqing Wang, Hehan Li, Peizhi Xu, Hanmeng Liu, Shuanglong Li, Xin Pei, Fuzhen Zhuan...
papers.summary: Latent reasoning for generative recommendation usually needs a teacher model to write chain-of-thought traces, which is costly and hard to stabilize. This paper skips teacher generation. It builds semantic targets from the text meaning of items already in a user's history, and uses those targets to supervise the model's intermediate tokens that are reserved for reasoning steps, without looking at the next-item label. With supervised fine-tuning alone, the method outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. On Beauty, it improves NDCG@1 by 20.6% and NDCG@5 by 10.3% over MiniOneRec. Controlled ablations indicate that the gain comes from input-matched historical semantic supervision, not from extra tokens by themselves.

papers.title: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Wendong Zhang, Weipeng Huang, Zhixin Ma, Bin Zhang, Dimin Wang
papers.summary: When a large model plans a recommendation workflow, it can be given memory of how a group of users has behaved. The difficulty is that new transaction feedback arrives the next day and the advice should change, while the record of the group definition, the observation window and the statistics must not be rewritten along the way. RecGroupMemory splits the memory in two layers. One is a read-only record of observations and the other is a profile with advice. The previous day's feedback may change only the second layer, and a check confirms the observations are unchanged, otherwise the original record is kept. In online comparisons on low-purchasing-power users chosen by the business team at an e-commerce platform, the group using memory alone had 1.58% more transacting users than its no-memory baseline. The group that added feedback revision had 1.78% more than its own no-memory baseline.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
papers.summary: Large language models are attractive rerankers, but running an expensive model on every request is costly and often hurts users with short histories. This production system, deployed for content recommendation at a large financial-planning software provider, reranks every request with a lightweight first tier. A router then uses segment cues such as history length to escalate only the requests more likely to benefit to a more expensive second tier, such as a larger model or multi-path reasoning. In a production experiment lasting over a month, it cut inference cost by about 10% versus using the expensive tier uniformly, with little latency impact and no observed quality regression. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Electronics, uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and the only statistically significant gain appears among users with the longest histories.

papers.title: Preprocessing Choices in Fine-Tuning Data Matter: Utility and Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.authors: Furkan Yasir Goksu, Yaren Yilmaz, Sule Gunduz Oguducu
papers.summary: When a large model generates recommendation lists directly, the way the fine-tuning data is preprocessed noticeably affects the results. The authors fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MovieLens-1M and compare choices. Even how a movie title is written matters. Moving a trailing article back to the front, so that Matrix, The becomes The Matrix, gives an HR@10 of 10.67%. Keeping the dataset's original form gives 12.47%. Balancing the training data to even out results across groups also depends on the attribute. Balancing by age narrows the utility gap between age groups and leaves overall utility almost unchanged. Balancing by gender lowers overall utility, and the utility gap between men and women does not shrink. Preprocessing choices should be judged on utility, output behavior and demographic sensitivity together.

papers.title: Generative Chain of Behavior for User Trajectory Prediction
papers.authors: Chengkai Huang, Xiaodi Chen, Hongtao Huang, Quan Z. Sheng, Lina Yao
papers.summary: Most sequential recommenders predict only a user's next item, yet user behavior is a chain of actions in which later steps depend on earlier ones. Generative Chain of Behavior (GCB) predicts several future behaviors directly. It first encodes each item as a Semantic ID of four discrete codes. The first three come from RQ-VAE quantizing the item vector level by level, with each level's codebook initialized by k-means clustering to avoid collapse, and the fourth only separates items whose codes collide, so semantically similar items share similar prefixes. A Transformer then generates the Semantic IDs of the next few steps autoregressively, each step conditioned on the steps already generated. On the Amazon Beauty and Cell Phones datasets, GCB is best or near-best on most multi-step metrics, with the clearest advantage on Cell Phones. The further ahead the prediction, the more every model degrades.

papers.title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
papers.authors: Sunkyung Lee, Xiaokai Wei, Da Long, Hyunsik Jeon, Jiajun Wu, Rithwik Seth, Jongwuk Lee, Michelle Gong, Gungor Polatkan
papers.summary: Generative recommenders can predict item identifiers from a user's history, but they rarely offer readable, concept-level control over what gets recommended, especially if the model cannot be retrained. This game-discovery work defines play concepts with a language model, finds sparse-autoencoder features that are both associated with a concept and effective when edited, and then amplifies or suppresses those features at inference time. On two industrial generative recommenders, amplification raises the share of the target concept by 113.6% on average for an Atomic ID model and by 24.6% for a Semantic ID model. Selecting features by their steering effect works better than picking the features most strongly associated with the concept.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.authors: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Fr...
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, retrieving the item a user wants does not mean the user sees it. The authors test this with Amazon review data and simulated users. Each simulated user has a target product in mind but may not name it, so it reveals requirements as the conversation goes. Each turn the system retrieves a batch of candidates and shows only the top 3. By the end of the dialogue the target has been retrieved in 74.75% of sessions, yet only 62.63% of sessions actually put it in front of the user, so the gap sits in choosing which candidates to show. The system itself splits work across several LLM agents: a supervisor asks clarifying questions when the request is vague and brings preferences from the user's earlier sessions into retrieval. Compared with one-shot recommendation, clarification plus memory raised the simulated users' acceptance rate by 28.9 percentage points. When evaluating conversational recommenders, the display step deserves its own measurement.

papers.title: SIDRec: End-to-End Semantic ID Representation and Modeling for Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuohang Jiang, Yongsen Pan, Pangjing Wu, Zihuai Zhao, Zheng Hu, Yuxin Chen
papers.summary: A Semantic ID (SID) is usually computed offline by quantizing a product's content vector, and it stays fixed while the ranking model is trained. This causes two problems. First, two products with similar content may attract different users, and the SID carries no such collaborative information. Second, how products are split into SIDs has never been trained against the click-prediction objective. SIDRec initializes a collaborative representation from the embeddings of a trained ranking model and keeps updating it during training, then fuses it with the content representation. It also lets quantization receive gradients. The forward pass still uses the discrete SID, while the backward pass uses a smooth probability approximation, so the click-prediction gradient reaches the quantizer and updates its parameters, which changes each product's SID assignment. On three public datasets it beats every compared method on AUC and GAUC, by up to 5.15% relative to the strongest baseline. Removing both the fusion and the end-to-end optimization lowers AUC by 7.19%.

papers.title: STCRank: Spatio-temporal Collaborative Ranking for Interactive Recommender System at Kuaishou E-shop
papers.authors: Boyang Xia, Ruilin Bao, Hanjun Jiang, Jun Wang, Wenwu Ou
papers.summary: In a full-screen e-commerce feed where each swipe down brings the next item, the two ranking objectives of whether the user buys and whether they keep swiping fight each other. Kuaishou E-shop's data show that after a purchase, users leave right away without swiping 61.3% of the time. With the usual labels, every one of those purchases becomes a negative sample for the swipe objective, so the learned swipe score ends up pushing down the items that sell. The authors drop purchase-then-exit samples from the swipe negatives. Ranking also stops picking the top-scoring item one screen at a time. Instead it scores different orderings of the next few items: each item's value is multiplied by the probability that the user swipes far enough to reach it, and the ordering with the highest total wins. Adding this look-ahead ranking to the full-screen feed alone raised online purchases by 2.10%. Teams running immersive feeds should check their objectives for conflicting labels first.

papers.title: SparseLift: Automatically Optimizing Opaque Sparse Paths in Industrial-Scale Recommendation Model Training
papers.authors: Changqing Shi, Anan Liu, Genbao Chen, Junchao Yang
papers.summary: In recommendation training, the embedding lookups and cross-GPU communication (the paper calls this the sparse path) appear in the computation graph as opaque nodes. A compiler cannot see inside them, so it cannot optimize them together with the computation around them. SparseLift first uses the model structure and runtime information to rebuild each opaque node as an analyzable subgraph. A cost model then checks, against the current execution plan, whether each candidate optimization actually pays off, and the chosen ones are assembled into a plan that later steady-state steps reuse. On a video-platform recommendation task with 100B sparse parameters, steady-state throughput on 8 GPUs rises by 16.5%. Switching optimizations off one at a time shows that running some sparse work early, so downstream steps wait less, matters most: removing it adds 12.7% to step time.

papers.title: IncVNM: An Interactive Recommender System with Incremental von Neumann-Morgenstern Utility Learning
papers.authors: Jiaxin Wei, Jia Liu
papers.summary: For products with random payoffs, such as stocks or insurance, whether a user likes one depends on the whole payoff distribution and on how much risk the user can tolerate. A recommender that learns one score per product goes stale when the distribution shifts. IncVNM learns a utility function for each user, which describes how that person trades risk against return. After the user clicks within a displayed list, the click order is turned into pairwise comparisons, where a product clicked earlier is preferred to one clicked later or not clicked, and the model changes its previous estimate as little as possible to satisfy them. The next list is chosen by scoring products with the current utility estimate and then sampling with entropy regularization. High scorers are more likely to be picked, but the top scorers are not always the only ones shown, so users choose among more varied products and give the model new comparisons. The authors simulate a risk-averse user on 463 S&P 500 stocks over 29 rolling windows. Under every click-noise level tested, IncVNM beats the expected-return, mean-variance, discounted UCB and BPR-variant baselines.

papers.title: Multicriteria Recommendation System by Leveraging Predefined, Implicit, and Undefined Criteria
papers.authors: Emrul Hasan, Chen Ding
papers.summary: A hotel's rating form lists only a few criteria such as location, service and value, but users also write in their reviews about things the form leaves out, like breakfast and noise. This paper splits each review into sentences and computes how similar each sentence is to every predefined criterion with sentence embeddings. A sentence goes to the criterion it most resembles, and sentiment analysis turns it into an implicit rating for that criterion. A sentence that is not similar enough to any predefined criterion (similarity below 0.3) is treated as an undefined aspect and also gets its own rating. A neural network then takes the predefined, implicit and undefined ratings together to predict the overall rating. On TripAdvisor the MSE is 3.08% lower than the strongest baseline, MRRRec, and on Beer Advocate it is 3.65% lower. The gain is modest, but dropping any of the three kinds of rating raises the error.

papers.title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
papers.authors: Jiwoo Choi, In Ik Lee, Woo Sung Seo, Minho Lee, Yun Young Choi
papers.summary: Before an ad campaign launches there are no historical logs, so cold-start performance is hard to estimate. When large language models simulate persona-conditioned user responses, what matters is which signals go into the prompt, not how richly the persona is written. On real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic groups, the method anchors on basic demographics without noisy extra attributes. The prompt notes that users often ignore banner ads even when the product seems relevant, instead of inserting numeric click-through rates. Mean absolute error between predicted and observed clicks across ad groups is 24.9 clicks. That is 51.3% lower than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM setup that uses explicit click-through-rate anchors. Minimal demographic descriptions also produce lower mean error than richer persona configurations.

papers.title: A Common Language for Dynamic Graphs: Interaction Tokenization Enables Foundation Models
papers.authors: Fuyuan Ma, Yili Wang, Xin He, Xin Zhang, Ying Wang, Xin Wang
papers.summary: A common task on dynamic graphs is predicting the next interaction, for example which item a user will visit next, and today each dataset usually gets its own separately trained model. This paper tries to build one pretrained model that works across datasets. For each query, the history before it is turned into one row of tabular features: who has contacted whom repeatedly, which intermediate nodes connect them indirectly, and which destinations were visited in what order. An existing tabular foundation model can read such rows directly, so no dedicated graph encoder has to be trained. The authors then keep training that model on a large set of synthetic dynamic graphs. On a real graph it uses labeled samples from the training period as context and updates no parameters. Across 13 datasets in TGB and TGB-Seq, CL-DGFM has the highest MRR on 10, beating the strongest baseline by 15.24 points on Flickr, and it is slightly behind TPNet on Wiki.

papers.title: Multi-criteria Rating and Review based Recommendation Model
papers.authors: Emrul Hasan, Chen Ding, Alfredo Cuzzocrea
papers.summary: A user rates a hotel on a few criteria such as value, service and cleanliness and also writes a comment. How should the two be combined to predict the overall rating? Earlier models used either the criteria ratings or the aspect ratings extracted from the text. MRRRec uses both. It estimates an implicit rating for each aspect from the comment, fills in criteria the user left unrated by predicting them from the ones that were filled in, and merges everything with attention. On TripAdvisor, against baselines such as ANR and DeepCoNN, MSE is on average 19% lower. In the ablation, dropping the criteria ratings and using only the review raises MSE by 7.7%, while dropping the review and using only the criteria ratings raises it by just 0.6%. So most of the gain comes from the criteria ratings, and the review text adds a smaller part. The authors also admit the model cannot yet tell which aspect in a review corresponds to which criteria rating.

papers.title: Simple Meta-Learning for HPO and CASH Using Performance Representations
papers.authors: Emiel Witting, Cheng Yan, Tom Julian Viering
papers.summary: To pick an algorithm and tune its hyperparameters for a new tabular task, people usually use Bayesian optimization. But when the hyperparameters of every algorithm are concatenated into one input, the dimension is high and, for any single configuration, most dimensions are inactive, which is hard to learn. This paper describes a configuration differently. It does not use the hyperparameter values. It uses the vector of scores that configuration got on earlier tasks, much like describing an item by the ratings users gave it in a recommender. Paired with plain Bayesian ridge regression, on the TabArena task of choosing an algorithm and tuning it, it reaches in 73 evaluations the level that ABLR needs 149 evaluations to reach, close to half the trials. Fitting is also far faster, under 3 seconds per task, against about two hours for GP-Hyper. When tuning only a single XGBoost model, ABLR is still best and this method ranks second.

papers.title: Adapting LLM Judges to Observed Human Annotation Policy through Soft Prompt Tuning
papers.authors: Tamás Janusko, Sven Kleinkop, Ricardo Bochnia, Gunnar Hempel, Steffen Tomschke, Jürgen Anke, Maik Thiele
papers.summary: An open-source small model used as a judge for chatbot replies often scores differently from human annotators. This paper freezes the model's parameters and trains only a short sequence of learnable vectors (a soft prompt) placed before the textual rubric, so the judge picks up the annotators' scoring habits. Training and testing use FairBotBench, a benchmark of e-commerce customer-service chats where humans rate each reply for bias, toxicity and personalization. Measured by agreement with human ratings (Krippendorff's alpha), Qwen 3.5 0.8B on toxicity starts out negatively correlated with human ratings and reaches 0.735 after tuning. After tuning, Qwen 3.5 9B beats the two hosted reference judges on all three dimensions. The authors caution that the size of the gain, and whether to keep the textual rubric, vary with the model and the task, so it should be re-validated on your own judge model.

papers.title: TabAbax: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
papers.authors: Zhixiong Cheng, Xiaoyun Gao, Shiyuan Han, Jingjing Suo, Zhengli Wang
papers.summary: To make a tabular foundation model predict better, deepening the in-context-learning Transformer helps very little, and the room lies upstream of it. TabAbax changes two things on top of TabICLv2. One is the synthetic tables used for pretraining. The number of categories in categorical features matches the preset value exactly. Category proportions are drawn from several distributions such as Dirichlet. Regression targets are no longer passed through a monotone stretching of their values after generation, so the target keeps the smooth relation to the features that the generation produced. The other is the encoder. It lets the rows within each column attend to one another and then the columns within each row, and that pair of steps now runs twice instead of once. On the regression benchmark Elo is 336 above TabICLv2, and swapping in only the new synthetic data adds 228, so most of the gain comes from the quality of the pretraining data.

papers.title: SPARSEUP: Towards Better Recipes for Training Modern Learned Sparse Retrievers
papers.authors: Thibault Formal, Pierre Erbacher, Cosimo Rulli
papers.summary: Sparse retrievers like SPLADE, moved onto newer backbones such as ModernBERT, often train poorly, and RoBERTa does not train at all. The authors trace this to the starting point: most of the new backbones' vocabulary scores are already positive, so at the start of training almost every term is active, the document representation is dense, and the gradient that tells terms apart weakens. The fix has three steps. Before training, one constant is subtracted from all scores, set at a high percentile of the score distribution estimated on a small sample of documents. Each input position may activate at most 12 terms. Case and word-boundary variants of the same word are merged. The final model reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, only 1.5 points below a dense model trained on the same backbone and data. Anyone moving sparse retrieval to a new backbone can start with these three steps.

papers.title: Interpretable Text Embeddings Based on Hierarchical Questions
papers.authors: Kohei Oda, Po-Min Chuang, Kiyoaki Shirai, Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn
papers.summary: Representing a text by its yes or no answers to a list of questions gives an embedding whose every dimension can be read, but with hundreds or thousands of questions, people cannot examine them all. This paper builds a hierarchy over the questions so that people only need to read a few broad ones to interpret an embedding, with task performance largely maintained. The questions are produced like this. A large text corpus is first clustered into a few broad groups, and an LLM contrasts the groups to write questions that tell them apart. Each group is then clustered into smaller groups and questions are written again, so shallow questions are broad and deep ones are specific and more numerous. Each deep question is attached to a broader shallow question (for illustration, a question about running sits under one about exercise). The paper also finds that, for the same number of questions, shallow questions give better embeddings than deep ones.

papers.title: Semantic Prior-Guided Incomplete Cross-Modal Retrieval with Noisy Labels
papers.authors: Jiali Chen, Ruitao Pu, Yingke Chen, Dezhong Peng
papers.summary: Cross-modal retrieval, such as searching images with text or text with images, is often trained on data where some samples lack one modality, and the class labels contain errors. Existing methods treat labels as the semantic reference, so a wrong label makes the filled-in content wrong too. SPIRN gives each class a fixed, mutually orthogonal reference vector that is not updated during training. The closer a sample is to the reference vector of its own label, the more it counts as clean and the larger its weight. After a while, every sample's label is changed to the class of its most similar reference vector. To fill a missing modality, the modality the sample has is used to find similar samples in a memory bank of complete samples, and their representations in the other modality are averaged with similarity weights. The closer a filled-in representation is to the reference vector of its class, the more confident the fill. At first only high-confidence fills are used, and less confident ones are admitted gradually as training goes on. It beats 11 existing methods in most settings on four datasets.

papers.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
papers.authors: Laurin Schmid, Suman Navaratnarajah, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Steffen Eger, Josif Grabocka, Christian Frey
papers.summary: Ask "What is the nationality of the director of Titanic?" If retrieval can return only one document, which one helps more? Intuition says the one holding the answer, the document stating that director James Cameron is Canadian. The authors find that keeping the bridge document, the one stating that Cameron directed the film, often works better, especially for smaller models: once the model knows whom to look up, it can often fill in the missing fact from its own memory. To run such comparisons, they built a multi-hop QA set, FondueQA, where each needed fact appears in exactly one designated document, so documents can be removed one at a time. The more popular the entity behind a missing fact, the more easily models fill it in. But adding a few plausible competing entities to the context can cut some models' accuracy by about 15 percentage points. In RAG, besides how much is retrieved, it matters which link of the reasoning chain is kept.

papers.title: EAGR: Evidence-Guided Adaptive Graph Retrieval
papers.authors: Sonam Gupta, Vignesh P, Vishwajeet Kumar, Adnan Qidwai, Anand Eswaran, Jaydeep Sen, Sachindra Joshi
papers.summary: Ask who someone's mother-in-law is, and a first retrieval rarely finds the answer: you first need the passage about their spouse, then follow the spouse to her mother. Where to search next only becomes clear once intermediate evidence arrives. Common approaches either build a knowledge graph in advance or have an LLM rewrite the query at every step. The first needs a separate store to build and maintain, the second adds a round of work per step. At ingestion, EAGR has an LLM extract descriptors such as entities from each passage and stores them as ordinary metadata in the vector database, so passages sharing a descriptor count as neighbors. At query time, dense retrieval finds a few starting passages. The LLM reads the evidence so far, picks the descriptors worth following, fetches neighboring passages through the metadata, and stops once the evidence suffices. Averaged over three multi-hop QA datasets, LLM-judged accuracy is 67.1%, against 59.8% for vanilla RAG and 63.2% for the strongest graph-based baseline.

papers.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
papers.authors: Zohreh Abbasi Liasi, Batoul Hammoud, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari
papers.summary: RAG assumes the model reasons over the relations stated in its context rather than falling back on associations memorized in pretraining. This paper tests exactly that in isolation, with the facts placed directly in the prompt and no retrieval. The multiple-choice questions start from Wikidata relations and come at five levels, remember, understand, apply, analyze, and evaluate, and were run on dozens of models in six languages. At the analyze level the model must rule out near-miss relations by checking them against the stated fact. At the evaluate level it must judge which statement is the relation's defining criterion, and checking against the fact cannot reject the distractors. Accuracy falls off a cliff from the apply level to the analyze level in every open-weight model series, by as much as 47.2 points, but not for either Gemini model. The evaluate level is a bottleneck too: Gemini 3.1 Pro averages 99.5% on the other four levels but only 60.7% on evaluate. A stronger model does not guarantee reliable reasoning over the evidence you give it.

papers.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Jyotin Goel, Abhinav Arun, Tejas Prakash Agarwal, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
papers.summary: GraphRAG retrieval strategies are usually tied to their own graph-construction pipeline, and few people test whether they still work when the graph is built differently. This paper finds that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph. When answering a question, ArcRAG starts from the entities the question names, assembles on the spot the node labels, relation descriptions, and property names reachable from them, plans multi-hop traversals against that interface, executes them as Cypher, and repairs them on failure. The same retrieval configuration works on a graph with typed nodes and a closed relation set, and on an untyped graph produced by open information extraction. On the open graph, MuSiQue EM is 38.0, which is 6.0 below the structured graph. On the structured graph it is 44.0, above every system reported in the paper's table. Construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

papers.title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment
papers.authors: Vihan Lakshman, Peter Baile Chen, Zhuohan Gu, Michael Cafarella
papers.summary: Small models are limited in what they can understand when doing RAG, and having a large model read documents online is too expensive. CacheGraft works offline and only once per corpus passage. It borrows the existing Cache-to-Cache fusion method: a trained fuser network merges, layer by layer, the KV cache a larger model builds from the passage into the cache the small model builds from the same passage. The result lives in the small model's own KV space and is stored. At query time, the relevant passage is chosen by embedding similarity, the small model loads its fused cache directly, and the question is read as text, so no large model is needed online. The test covers five QA benchmarks, with either the top retrieved passage or the gold passage as context. Answers are scored by two LLM judges and by whether they contain the correct answer. Answer quality beats the text-only small model in 29 of 30 comparisons, by up to about 8 points, and the fuser was never trained on retrieval data. It is worth a look where only a small model can be deployed.

papers.title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
papers.authors: Dikshant Kukreja, Gautam Gupta, Avni Mittal, Avinash Anand, Kritarth Prasad, Zhengkui Wang, Timothy Liu, Rajiv Ratn Shah...
papers.summary: When a prompt contains irrelevant content, such as statements from unrelated domains or random tokens, the model gets answers wrong. This is common in RAG, tool use, and long context, yet the cause had not been explained. This paper traces an interference path inside the model and finds a few attention heads, which it calls intrusion heads. They write irrelevant content into the prediction position and promote distractor-related content, and the correct answer receives weaker support as a result. The intrusion heads are largely disjoint from the heads that integrate useful context. Replacing the corrupted last-token representation with its clean version recovers 97.6% of the distractor-induced accuracy drop on average, but that needs an extra clean forward pass and cannot be deployed. The deployable fix is to knock out about ten intrusion heads, roughly 1% of all attention heads, which recovers 57%.

papers.title: Weaver: Weaving Preference Evidence through Incremental Reasoning for Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Linyao Zheng, Zhifang Mao, Xuhang Shi
papers.summary: Personalized RAG has to find a user's preferences in very long conversation histories, which is hard for two reasons. The evidence is scattered across conversations, so no single fragment is complete, and preferences depend on time and situation, so they are easily mixed up. Weaver first has an LLM split the current request into interdependent subquestions, and the information a subquestion still lacks is a gap. For example, a request to recommend an activity can split into which activity settings the user prefers and how they feel in crowds. Each time it finds a clue, it uses that clue to locate the next missing piece of evidence instead of retrieving everything at once. It then reads the evidence together to decide which preferences apply to the current situation and which conflict, and updates what is still missing. It reaches 86.42% accuracy on PersonaMem, 16.01 points above the strongest baseline, and 91.10% on PrefEval.

papers.title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving
papers.authors: Akshat Valse, Ali Jannesari
papers.summary: Multi-turn LLM agents rely on prefix caching to skip repeated work, but this paper finds a trap. After a sudden burst of sessions, an engine can fall into a state where every turn misses the cache and the backlog never drains, even at a load it handled before. In paired tests on two serving engines, two GPUs and two models, a burst of 200 sessions left the engine stuck to the end in all 30 runs, while every matched run without a burst stayed healthy. The authors model the stuck state as a queue in which every turn misses and derive how the backlog grows. The way out is simple: capping the number of concurrent sessions rescues an already trapped engine at the same load. Agent serving has to guard against bursts that wipe out the cache, not just watch average load.

papers.title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building
papers.authors: Tobias Rubel, Richard Wen, Guy Blelloch, Laxman Dhulipala, Lars Gottesbüren, Jakub Łącki, Vahab Mirrokni
papers.summary: Graph indexes for vector search, such as HNSW and Vamana, answer queries fast but take hours or even days to build on large datasets. PiPNN speeds this up by splitting the vectors into small blocks, finding neighbors inside each block with matrix multiplication, and merging the results into one graph. This paper pushes that route further. It quantizes the vectors to low precision to cut memory traffic, and it fuses the matrix multiplication with picking the top K neighbors, so the full distance matrix is never written back to memory. On CPUs, index building is up to 8 times faster than the original PiPNN. On GPUs it is up to 50 times faster than CAGRA, with query performance at high recall matching or beating the baselines. Teams that rebuild vector indexes often may no longer be held back by build time.

papers.title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
papers.authors: Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou
papers.summary: Large-scale embedding clustering still often uses Lloyd's k-means, which takes many epochs and is awkward to tune. This paper turns the updates into mini-batches with an exponential moving average, and it gives scaling rules that set the decay rate and batch size from the number of clusters and the dataset size, so those knobs can be set without a hyperparameter sweep. Across embedding datasets, it reaches the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in about two to three epochs, which translates to 10 to 45 times faster GPU wall-clock time than strong existing implementations. As one example, it partitions very large DINO embedding collections into many millions of clusters in just a few epochs, with a loss below Lloyd's longer training run.

papers.title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
papers.authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
papers.summary: Decode attention streams the key-value cache for every newly generated token. Packing that cache into low-bit integers reduces memory traffic, but it does not automatically save latency, because converting each value and applying scale and offset before the Tensor Cores saturates instruction-issue throughput. This method leaves those per-value fixes off the cached values. It folds the scale and offset onto the other matrix operand or the product output, depending on the quantization scheme, and preserves the dequantized attention result in exact arithmetic. On H100, the INT2 and INT4 kernels reach geo-mean speedups of 3.36 times and 2.83 times over FlashInfer BF16.

papers.title: ResServe: Accurate and Efficient FP4 LLM Inference with Residue Compensation
papers.authors: Shuo Rong, Ruibo Fan, Jiawen Wen, Xiaowen Chu
papers.summary: Block-scaled 4-bit floating-point inference lowers the cost of large language models but can hurt task quality. Decode matrices are often narrow, which leaves spare hardware capacity. This system keeps an FP4 activation base plus an FP4-quantized residue that represents what quantization discarded, uses the spare capacity to compute the residue on chip, and adds it back without extra result transfers. On NVIDIA B200, the extra request latency is at most 3.4% over uncompensated 4-bit weights and activations, while request latency falls 22.4% to 53.3% relative to 4-bit weights with 8-bit activations. Across five models, code-generation accuracy improves by a mean of 15.04% relative to same-format inference without compensation.

papers.title: A Controlled Experimental Evaluation of Configuration and Cache Architecture in LLM Serving Engines
papers.authors: Muhammad Faizan Anwar, Sina Keshvadi
papers.summary: Benchmarks often report that SGLang is far faster than vLLM and credit its prefix-cache design. This paper finds that comparisons of default deployments mix in another setting: whether a long prompt is prefilled in chunks. Under defaults on a multi-agent workload, vLLM's median time to first token is up to 64 times SGLang's. Matching chunked prefill alone removes 78% of the gap in sustained throughput where that gap is largest, and the gap in time to first token shrinks clearly too. What remains after matching is a real tail-latency advantage for SGLang at equal throughput, consistent with ordering waiting requests by what is cached. When comparing serving engines, match the configuration first, then judge the cache architecture.

papers.title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
papers.authors: Rahul Sharma, Nitin Vegesna, Yanxin Zhang
papers.summary: Reinforcement-learning post-training burns a lot of power, yet the GPU does not need to run at full clock all the time. Generation emits one token at a time and is often limited by memory bandwidth, and time spent waiting on other GPUs burns power too, so lowering the clock barely slows it down. This NVIDIA work builds an online controller, EE-RL, that picks separate GPU frequencies for generation and for training. It predicts how the default governor would perform on the same token workload, runs a few short trials, keeps the most energy-efficient setting that holds at least 98% of default throughput, and keeps adjusting as the workload changes. With training and generation on separate GPU pools in synchronous mode, it saves up to 16.9% of GPU energy at only 1.4% lower throughput. The power bill drops without touching the algorithm.

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
papers.authors: Jia Wei, Ziyi Qiu, Yi Xu, Xuehai Qian
papers.summary: When an MoE model is trained with reinforcement learning, response generation is often held up by the few longest responses. A GPU whose own responses are finished still cannot be released, because the experts are spread across GPUs and unfinished responses elsewhere may call on the experts it holds. The paper measures that about one third of occupied time in the baseline comes after a GPU's own responses are done. FlexFloor first predicts from historical response lengths how long each response will take and groups prompts of similar expected length so they finish at about the same time. Finished GPUs then leave the expert-parallel group, the experts are rearranged across the remaining GPUs so that together they still hold every expert, and enough KV cache space is kept. Generation throughput rises by 52.74%, about 65.40% more tokens are generated per unit of occupied compute time, and rollout reward barely changes.

papers.title: DARIC: A Position-Independent KV Cache Reuse System with Distribution-Aware Recomputation
papers.authors: Weikang Wang, Haiyang Liu, Xin Zhou, Jun Liu, Weifeng Zhang
papers.summary: As contexts grow, reusing key-value caches across requests without tying them to the original token positions can speed up the first generated token, but some tokens usually have to be recomputed to restore interactions across chunks. Existing methods often ignore how far a reused cache has drifted from a fully recomputed one, so token selection is either expensive or harmful to quality, and they may require a custom execution path in the serving engine. This system chooses what to recompute from that deviation distribution and keeps cache generation and recomputation loosely coupled. In an agentic coding setting it matches the pass rate of full recomputation while making TTFT 2.1 times faster; on some long-context retrieval-question datasets the speedup reaches 8.2 times.

papers.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
papers.authors: Hongseung Yu, In Gim, Kyunghan Lee, Lin Zhong
papers.summary: When a large MoE model runs locally, the GPU cannot hold every expert, so missing experts are fetched from host memory during inference. The usual remedy is prefetching, which fetches the experts the next layers will probably need while the link is idle. The authors find that prefetching can backfire when the GPU keeps an expert cache. The more needed experts the cache already holds, the harder the remaining ones are to guess, and wrong guesses waste bandwidth and memory. Bevy schedules instead of guessing. It runs several requests at once, and a request whose experts are ready runs ahead to later layers, revealing exactly which experts it needs next, so fetching overlaps with computing. On two local platforms its decode throughput reaches up to 1.55 times that of the fastest prefetching baseline. For local MoE serving, ordering requests well can beat predicting experts.

papers.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
papers.authors: Tan Sang Nguyen, Yi Ru Wang, Shailesh Shailesh, Gang Yang, Jiamo Hu, Jianuo Jiang, Haoquan Fang, Zhongzheng Ren, Zhongyi...
papers.summary: Ranking general-purpose robot policies is hard because real-robot experiments are difficult to reproduce: change the site or the object layout and the result changes. RoboColosseum tests five robot foundation models and three frontier LLM agents head to head on four robot types at many real sites, with both models facing the same local conditions. Frontier agents match models specialized for robots, but every system struggles to finish open-world tasks reliably. Success alone hides differences: on the G1 humanoid no policy completed any task, yet each task has several preset completion conditions and progress is the share met, and average progress still ranged from 13.3% to 23.2%. ==Rankings agree only weakly across different robots==, so evaluation should span several robots and look at progress.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jea...
papers.summary: Robot manipulation does not have to rely on specialist policies trained on large sets of demonstrations. In this paper a generalist AI model acts as an agent, commands the robot arm directly and adjusts as the task unfolds, with no demonstrations and no task-specific training, and it succeeds far more often than specially trained VLA policies. The authors' reference harness, AMP1, reaches an 85.6% zero-shot success rate on the RoboLab-120 benchmark, against 49.2% for the leading VLA policy, and it succeeds in nearly all real-robot trials across three robots and twelve tasks. The harness supplies no grasping, pushing or placing skills, so the agent works out its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools and calibrating its cameras. A generalist model used directly as the controller may be more general and more robust than a specially trained policy.

papers.title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Luca Macesanu, Tianluo Zhang, Aditya Patil, Archit Sharma, Kevin Angers, Christopher M. Clark, Chen Feng, Juexiao Zhang
papers.summary: Robot foundation models can adapt from demonstrations placed in context, without further fine-tuning. Retrieval that relies on visual similarity alone may not match the current stage of execution. This method estimates task-relative progress from a reference demonstration video, a language instruction, and the current observation, then uses that progress to retrieve demonstration context. Conditioning on a reference video lets it align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen in training. On real-world manipulation tasks, success rises from 6.2% for a fine-tuned baseline to 23.8%.

papers.title: Horizon-Coupled Obstacle Guidance for Relative-Action Diffusion Policies
papers.authors: Guangyuan Wang, Haishan Xia, Zitao Zhang, Kejia Chen, Yuanchen Sun, Zhenguo Sun, Donghao Zhang, Yu Zhang, Alois Knoll
papers.summary: After deployment, a robot often has to avoid obstacles it never saw in training, without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often corrects each horizon step on its own, which can fix a local violation without assembling a complete, task-directed detour. This inference-time method guides a pretrained relative-action diffusion policy by rolling cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, scoring obstacle interactions along that path with a signed-distance model, and sending each obstacle response back to all contributing action increments during denoising. In seven obstacle-constrained scenes across four manipulation tasks, it completes 75.0% of trials without collision, compared with 5.7% for absolute-action point-wise guidance.

papers.title: HITCH: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Operate a Humanoid through a Whole-Body Harness
papers.authors: Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Xinming Wang, Liu Cao, Yanjiang Guo, Mengdi Xu, Jianyu Chen
papers.summary: Letting a VLM drive a humanoid robot has two hurdles: the model must tell where objects are and how far away, and the robot must turn high-level commands such as reach there or turn the torso into stable whole-body motion. HITCH gives the VLM an interface for both. The VLM picks a point in its image and gets back the 3D position of that point; it issues commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking and gaze, and a learned controller turns them into whole-body motion. Measuring the scene accurately and executing commands accurately each raise task success. Teacher policies then solve five base tasks through this interface, and a VLM fine-tuned on those trajectories goes from 3.3% to 51.1% success on SIMPLE without any SIMPLE trajectories. On a real G1 it carried a box in 13 of 20 trials with no real training data.

papers.title: STEP: Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
papers.authors: Youhao Lyu, Chenghao Sun, Zhenxuan Ding, Shuting Zhang, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
papers.summary: A humanoid climbing stairs or crossing gaps reads the terrain through a depth camera, but which part of the terrain matters depends on the robot's own body state and on how both change after each action. Existing methods either fuse visual and body-sensing features or predict one signal from the other at the same moment, and neither directly constrains how the state changes after an action. STEP adds two prediction tasks during training. It hides one signal and predicts its features from the other, and it predicts the next fused state from the current state and the executed action. On a real robot it succeeds in 98 of 100 trials across stairs, a high platform, a wide gap, stepping stones and walking backward on stairs, where it cannot see the terrain behind it. When camera input drops out or lags, both prediction tasks also keep the policy steadier.

papers.title: MessyNav: Zero-Shot Navigation via Manipulation in Messy Environments
papers.authors: Kenneth Llontop, Cherie Ho, Dylan Zhou, Anuva Banwasi, Priya Sundaresan, Carlota Parés-Morlans, Jeannette Bohg
papers.summary: In homes and offices, paths are often blocked by chairs, toys and carts, and a robot has to decide which objects it can push aside and which it must go around: an empty cart can be pushed, but one carrying fragile glassware cannot. MessyNav needs no training in simulation and no per-scene instructions. It first has a vision-language model judge, from the image and its context, whether each object can be swiped aside, picked up or should be avoided, and then plans actions from those labels. Across 15 real-world scenes it reached the goal without unsafe interactions 67% of the time, against 40% for planning with the same model when judgment and planning share one prompt. Separating the two helps because whether an object can move depends on its state, such as whether the stack on top is stable, and that should be settled before planning.

papers.title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
papers.authors: Vongani H. Maluleke, James Ni, Kie Horiuchi, Lea Wilken, Jiahui Lei, Evonne Ng, Roei Herzig, Jitendra Malik, Trevor Darr...
papers.summary: Most humanoid robots are trained alone, so they cannot coordinate with a person next to them: when someone reaches out for a hug or a high-five, the robot neither anticipates it nor adjusts. Social Humanoid has a Unitree G1 generate matching motion from a person's motion, such as a hug, or a greeting followed by posing for a photo together. It has two layers. A high-level model turns human and robot motion into the same set of discrete codes and generates the robot's response from them, and it can keep predicting the person's motion when they are occluded. A low-level controller then executes the motion on the robot. The training data come from transferring five human-human motion-capture datasets onto the robot, giving 260 hours of human-humanoid interaction. In simulation 90% to 100% of generated motions were executed fully by the low-level controller, and on the real G1 the success rate matched simulation in every scenario.

papers.title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
papers.authors: Dingkun Wei, Zehong Shen, Huaijin Pi, Xueyang Wang, Xing Zhu, Hujun Bao, Yujun Shen, Xiaowei Zhou
papers.summary: Humanoid whole-body control has to track diverse reference motions while staying balanced under gravity, torque limits, contact switches, and disturbances. Reinforcement-learning trackers often let one policy output both tracking and balance commands, even though similar reference poses can demand very different dynamics, which complicates learning and can produce high-frequency fluctuations. This framework splits the job. Inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint proportional-derivative feedback supply the tracking torques, and a residual policy learns only the extra joint-torque corrections needed for balanced execution. In simulation and on hardware, one learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets and keeps tracking and balance under attached payloads and physical disturbances. Across all evaluated training-data scales it achieves higher tracking accuracy and success rates than a retrained SONIC baseline.

papers.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
papers.authors: Arpit Bahety, Skand Peri, Sriniket Ambatipudi, Chen Xu, Haruki Nishimura, Masha Itkina, Roberto Martín-Martín
papers.summary: Robot manipulation foundation models fail after deployment, for example by colliding or dropping objects. The usual fix is to have a human take over, demonstrate a correction and fine-tune on the data, but that only teaches do this action in this scene, so it breaks when the scene changes and often needs tens to hundreds of interventions. OopsieRecover tries to learn from a handful of corrections what went wrong and how to avoid it. It has a vision-language model propose several possible reasons from the scene, the actions before and after takeover, and a spoken description, then checks them against all corrections and keeps the one that explains them best. That reason becomes a rule saying when it applies and which actions are penalized then, for example tilting a mug while placing it. At deployment the original model proposes several candidate actions and the one with the lowest penalty is chosen. On new scenes of the CoffeeMug task, 8 corrections were enough to reach 84% success, while HG-DAgger fine-tuned on three times as many corrections reached only 28%.
